metadata.title: A Simple Proof of the Johnson--Lindenstrauss Extension Theorem

nodes.name: Lipschitz constant
nodes.statement: The Lipschitz constant of a mapping $f:T\to Y$ between metric spaces is defined as $\Lip(f)=\sup_{x\ne y \in T} d_Y(f(x),f(y))/d_T(x,y)$.

nodes.name: Johnson--Lindenstrauss Lipschitz extension theorem
nodes.statement: Let $T$ be an arbitrary $n$-point metric space, and $X\supset T$ an arbitrary superspace. Let $\mathcal H$ be a Hilbert space and $f:T\to \mathcal H$ a mapping . Then there exists an extension $F:X\to \mathcal H$ of $f$ such that $F|_T=f$, and $\Lip(F) \lesssim \sqrt{\log n} \cdot \Lip(f)$.
assumptions: Let $T$ be an arbitrary $n$-point metric space, and $X\supset T$ an arbitrary superspace.
Let $\mathcal H$ be a Hilbert space and $f:T\to \mathcal H$ a mapping .
conclusions: Then there exists an extension $F:X\to \mathcal H$ of $f$ such that $F|_T=f$, and $\Lip(F) \lesssim \sqrt{\log n} \cdot \Lip(f)$.

nodes.name: McShane extension theorem
nodes.statement: Since $u_\omega:T\to \R$, by the McShane extension theorem (also known as the nonlinear Hahn--Banach theorem), $u_\omega$ can be extended to $U_\omega :X\to \mathbb \R$ such that $U_\omega|_T=u_\omega$, and $\Lip(U_\omega)=\Lip(u_\omega)$.
conclusions: $u_\omega$ can be extended to $U_\omega :X\to \mathbb \R$ such that $U_\omega|_T=u_\omega$, and $\Lip(U_\omega)=\Lip(u_\omega)$.

nodes.name: Expected maximum of squared standard Gaussians
nodes.statement: It is a classical and elementary fact that for $m\ge 2$ standard Gaussians $G_1,\ldots, G_m$, with any dependence structure, \begin{equation} \E [\max\{G_1^2,\ldots, G_m^2\}] \lesssim  \log m. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1 (Johnson--Lindenstrauss extension)
nodes.statement:
We may assume without loss of generality that $\mathcal H=\R^n$, i.e., $f:T	o \R^n$.  Furthermore, assume that by rescaling $\Lip(f)=1$. Let $g_1,\ldots, g_n$ be i.i.d. standard Gaussian random variables defined on a probability space $\Omega$, and consider the real-valued Hilbert space $H=L_2(\Omega)$. Consider the linear mapping $k:\R^n 	o H$ defined by \( k(x_1,\ldots,x_n)= \sum_{i=1}^n x_i g_i. \) It is a property of the Gaussian distribution that if $g_1,\ldots,g_n$ are independent standard Gaussian variables, then $\sum_{i=1}^n x_ig_i$ is a centered Gaussian random variable with variance $\sum_{i=1}^nx_i^2$, which means that $\|\sum_i x_i g_i\|_{L_2(\Omega)}=\|(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\|_2$. Hence $k$ is an isometric isomorphism of $\R^n$ in $k(\R^n) \subset H$. Thus, $u:=k\circ f:T 	o k(\R^n)$ is also 1-Lipschitz. We will use the notation $u=(u_\omega)_{\omega\in \Omega}$, and $k=(k_\omega)_{\omega\in\Omega}$. Fix $\omega\in \Omega$. Since $u_\omega:T	o \R$, by the McShane extension theorem (also known as the nonlinear Hahn--Banach theorem), $u_\omega$ can be extended to $U_\omega :X	o \mathbb \R$ such that $U_\omega|_T=u_\omega$, and $\Lip(U_\omega)=\Lip(u_\omega)$. The McShane extension is a simple result. For completeness, we provide a quick proof at the end of this note, see also~\cite[Theorem~1.33]{Weaver-Lip}. We thus obtain $U:=(U_\omega)_{\omega\in\Omega}:X	o H$, an extension of $u$. Using the orthogonal projection $P:H	o k(\mathbb \R^n)$, we see that $F:=k^{-1}\circ P\circ U:X	o \R^n$ is an extension of $f$. Since $\Lip(k^{-1})=\Lip(P)=1$, we have $\Lip(F) \le \Lip(U)$. We next bound $\Lip(U)$. For $x,y\in X$:  egin{align} 
onumber    \| U(x)-U(y)\|_{L_2(\Omega)} &= \Bigl (\E_\Omega  igl [|U_\omega(x)-U_\omega(y)|^2  igr ]\Bigr )^{1/2} \ 
onumber    &\le d(x,y) \Bigl (\E_\Omega [\Lip(U_\omega)^2]\Bigr )^{1/2} \ 
onumber    & = d(x,y) \Bigl (\E_\Omega [\Lip(u_\omega)^2]\Bigr )^{1/2} \ 
onumber & = d(x,y) \left ( \E_\Omega \max_{s
e t\in T} \Bigl( rac{\sum_i f(s)_i g_i(\omega)- \sum_i f(t)_i g_i(\omega)}{d(s,t)}\Bigr)^2 ight)^{1/2} \ 
onumber &\le d(x,y) iggl ( \E_\Omega \max_{s
e t\in T} \Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^n  rac{ f(s)_i-f(t)_i}{\|f(s)-f(t)\|_2} g_i(\omega)\Bigr)^2  iggr)^{1/2} \ &= d(x,y)\Bigl ( \E_\Omega \max_{ s
e t\in T}  G_{f(s)-f(t)}^2 \Bigr)^{1/2}, \end{align} where $G_{z}:= \sum_i  rac{z_i}{\|z\|_2} g_i$. $\{G_{f(s)-f(t)}\}_{s,t\in T}$ are standard Gaussians (but not necessarily stochastically independent). It is a classical and elementary fact that for $m\ge 2$ standard Gaussians $G_1,\ldots, G_m$, with any dependence structure,  egin{equation} \E [\max\{G_1^2,\ldots, G_m^2\}] \lesssim  \log m. \end{equation} For completeness, we provide a quick proof of~\eqref{eq:max-chi-sqaured} below. Since $|T|=n$, the maximum  in~\eqref{eq:max-gauss} is over at most $n^2$ squared Gaussians, and therefore~\eqref{eq:max-gauss} is bounded above by a constant times $d(x,y) \cdot \sqrt{\log n}$.

nodes.name: Reduce to $\R^n$ and set up a Gaussian Hilbert space
nodes.statement: We may assume without loss of generality that $\mathcal H=\R^n$, i.e., $f:T\to \R^n$.  Furthermore, assume that by rescaling $\Lip(f)=1$. Let $g_1,\ldots, g_n$ be i.i.d. standard Gaussian random variables defined on a probability space $\Omega$, and consider the real-valued Hilbert space $H=L_2(\Omega)$.

nodes.name: Embed $\R^n$ isometrically via Gaussians; $u=k\circ f$ is 1-Lipschitz
nodes.statement: Consider the linear mapping $k:\R^n \to H$ defined by \( k(x_1,\ldots,x_n)= \sum_{i=1}^n x_i g_i. \) It is a property of the Gaussian distribution that if $g_1,\ldots,g_n$ are independent standard Gaussian variables, then $\sum_{i=1}^n x_ig_i$ is a centered Gaussian random variable with variance $\sum_{i=1}^nx_i^2$, which means that $\|\sum_i x_i g_i\|_{L_2(\Omega)}=\|(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\|_2$. Hence $k$ is an isometric isomorphism of $\R^n$ in $k(\R^n) \subset H$. Thus, $u:=k\circ f:T \to k(\R^n)$ is also 1-Lipschitz. We will use the notation $u=(u_\omega)_{\omega\in \Omega}$, and $k=(k_\omega)_{\omega\in\Omega}$.

nodes.name: Extend each coordinate $u_\omega$ by McShane and assemble $F$
nodes.statement: Fix $\omega\in \Omega$. Since $u_\omega:T\to \R$, by the McShane extension theorem (also known as the nonlinear Hahn--Banach theorem), $u_\omega$ can be extended to $U_\omega :X\to \mathbb \R$ such that $U_\omega|_T=u_\omega$, and $\Lip(U_\omega)=\Lip(u_\omega)$. The McShane extension is a simple result. For completeness, we provide a quick proof at the end of this note, see also~\cite[Theorem~1.33]{Weaver-Lip}. We thus obtain $U:=(U_\omega)_{\omega\in\Omega}:X\to H$, an extension of $u$. Using the orthogonal projection $P:H\to k(\mathbb \R^n)$, we see that $F:=k^{-1}\circ P\circ U:X\to \R^n$ is an extension of $f$. Since $\Lip(k^{-1})=\Lip(P)=1$, we have $\Lip(F) \le \Lip(U)$.

onumber    &\le d(x,y) \Bigl (\E_\Omega [\Lip(U_\omega)^2]\Bigr )^{1/2} \ 
onumber    & = d(x,y) \Bigl (\E_\Omega [\Lip(u_\omega)^2]\Bigr )^{1/2} \ 
onumber & = d(x,y) \left ( \E_\Omega \max_{s

onumber &\le d(x,y) iggl ( \E_\Omega \max_{s
e t\in T} \Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^n  rac{ f(s)_i-f(t)_i}{\|f(s)-f(t)\|_2} g_i(\omega)\Bigr)^2  iggr)^{1/2} \ &= d(x,y)\Bigl ( \E_\Omega \max_{ s
e t\in T}  G_{f(s)-f(t)}^2 \Bigr)^{1/2}, \end{align} where $G_{z}:= \sum_i  rac{z_i}{\|z\|_2} g_i$. $\{G_{f(s)-f(t)}\}_{s,t\in T}$ are standard Gaussians (but not necessarily stochastically independent).

nodes.name: Apply the max-Gaussian bound to conclude the $\sqrt{\log n}$ factor
nodes.statement: It is a classical and elementary fact that for $m\ge 2$ standard Gaussians $G_1,\ldots, G_m$, with any dependence structure, \begin{equation} \E [\max\{G_1^2,\ldots, G_m^2\}] \lesssim  \log m. \end{equation} For completeness, we provide a quick proof of~\eqref{eq:max-chi-sqaured} below. Since $|T|=n$, the maximum  in~\eqref{eq:max-gauss} is over at most $n^2$ squared Gaussians, and therefore~\eqref{eq:max-gauss} is bounded above by a constant times $d(x,y) \cdot \sqrt{\log n}$.

nodes.name: Proof of the expected-maximum bound
nodes.statement: By a classical Gaussian tail bound, $\Pr[G_i\ge t] \le e^{-t^2/2}$, and therefore $\Pr[G_i^2\ge t] \le 2e^{-t/2}$.  By the union bound, $\Pr[ \max\{G_1^2,\ldots,G_m^2\}\ge t]\le 2me^{-t/2}$. For any $s\ge 0$, we can estimate $\E[\max\{G_1^2,\ldots,G_m^2\}]$ by partitioning the integral up to parameter $s\ge 0$ and from $s$ to $\infty$ as follows: \begin{multline*} \E[\max\{G_1^2,\ldots,G_m^2\}] \le s+ \int_s^\infty \Pr \left [\max\{G_1^2,\ldots,G_m^2\} \ge t\right ] dt\\ \le s+ \int_s^\infty 2m e^{-t/2}dt = s+4m e^{-s/2}. \end{multline*} Substituting $s=2\log m$ (and noting that $m\ge2$) proves~\eqref{eq:max-chi-sqaured}.

nodes.name: Gaussian tail bound and union bound on the maximum
nodes.statement: By a classical Gaussian tail bound, $\Pr[G_i\ge t] \le e^{-t^2/2}$, and therefore $\Pr[G_i^2\ge t] \le 2e^{-t/2}$.  By the union bound, $\Pr[ \max\{G_1^2,\ldots,G_m^2\}\ge t]\le 2me^{-t/2}$.

nodes.name: Partition the integral to estimate the expectation
nodes.statement: For any $s\ge 0$, we can estimate $\E[\max\{G_1^2,\ldots,G_m^2\}]$ by partitioning the integral up to parameter $s\ge 0$ and from $s$ to $\infty$ as follows: \begin{multline*} \E[\max\{G_1^2,\ldots,G_m^2\}] \le s+ \int_s^\infty \Pr \left [\max\{G_1^2,\ldots,G_m^2\} \ge t\right ] dt\\ \le s+ \int_s^\infty 2m e^{-t/2}dt = s+4m e^{-s/2}. \end{multline*}

nodes.name: Proof of McShane extension for finite domains
nodes.statement: Let $T\subset X$,  $T$ finite, and $q:T\to \mathbb R$ $L$-Lipschitz. Define $Q:X\to \mathbb R$ by \( Q(x) =\min_{t\in T} q(t)+ L d_X(x,t) \). It is left to the reader to check that $Q|_T=q$  using the Lipschitz condition on $q$. Next we prove the Lipshitz condition for $Q$. Fix $x,y\in X$, and let $t\in T$ satisfy $Q(x)=q(t)+L d_X(x,t)$. Applying the definition of $Q(y)$, and the triangle inequality in $X$, we have \[ Q(y)\le q(t)+Ld_X(y,t) \le q(t)+Ld_X(x,t)+Ld_X(x,y)= Q(x)+ Ld_X(x,y). \] Hence $Q(y)-Q(x)\le Ld_X(x,y)$. By symmetry, we also have $Q(x)-Q(y)\le Ld(x,y)$.
nodes.section: Proof of McShane extension for finite domains

nodes.name: Prove the Lipschitz bound for $Q$ via the triangle inequality
nodes.statement: Next we prove the Lipshitz condition for $Q$. Fix $x,y\in X$, and let $t\in T$ satisfy $Q(x)=q(t)+L d_X(x,t)$. Applying the definition of $Q(y)$, and the triangle inequality in $X$, we have \[ Q(y)\le q(t)+Ld_X(y,t) \le q(t)+Ld_X(x,t)+Ld_X(x,y)= Q(x)+ Ld_X(x,y). \] Hence $Q(y)-Q(x)\le Ld_X(x,y)$. By symmetry, we also have $Q(x)-Q(y)\le Ld(x,y)$.
